headline_marked: [[Saima Wazed resigns from WHO]] amid fraud probes and financial irregularities allegations
headline: Saima Wazed resigns from WHO amid fraud probes and financial irregularities allegations
summary: Saima Wazed has officially stepped down as the WHO Southeast Asia Regional Director following accusations of financial misconduct and providing false educational credentials. She had been on unpaid leave since July 2025.
details: Saima Wazed has formally resigned from her position as the World Health Organization's (WHO) Regional Director for Southeast Asia. Her resignation comes amidst allegations of financial irregularities and misrepresentation of educational qualifications.

She submitted her resignation letter to WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus on Wednesday, September 9, as confirmed by international news agency Reuters. Wazed was elected in November 2023 and began her five-year term in February 2024.

The allegations surfaced as part of an Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) investigation into corruption involving Sheikh Hasina and her family members, following the fall of the Awami League government in 2024. Subsequently, WHO sent Saima Wazed on unpaid leave in July 2025.

Reuters reported that WHO was investigating her over financial irregularities during a trip to China, providing incorrect information about her academic qualifications, and illegal plot acquisition in Bangladesh. Saima Wazed has denied all these allegations through her lawyers.

She claims that a $901 adjustment for the China trip was an administrative error by an assistant, and that she had previously informed the WHO chief that her doctorate degree was honorary. In her resignation letter, she stated a loss of trust in WHO leadership due to being prevented from effective duty.

Wazed also cited an unbearable financial situation after nearly a year without pay while on unpaid leave. WHO sources indicated that the process to formally remove her from the position was already underway. New nominations for the post are expected by October 12, with an election for the new regional director likely on January 24.

headline: Secret mobile phone data sold online; even ministers' info compromised for a fee
summary: Websites and social media groups are openly selling sensitive personal data, including Call Detail Records (CDRs), NID, and location information, for a fee. Even a Bangladeshi minister's private phone data was obtained, highlighting a severe privacy breach.
details: Sensitive personal data, including call records, messages, and location information, is being openly sold online in Bangladesh. This illicit trade operates through dedicated websites and social media platforms, making private information accessible for a fee.

Prothom Alo conducted an investigation, successfully acquiring the Call Detail Records (CDRs) of a Bangladeshi minister for a specified payment. The minister confirmed the accuracy of the obtained data, expressing shock and concern over the security implications.

The investigation further revealed that CDRs of two heads of crucial information technology and telecommunication agencies, along with two Prothom Alo staff members, were also obtainable and verified as accurate. This demonstrates the pervasive nature of the data breach across various sectors.

Beyond CDRs, the online black market offers a range of personal information, including National ID (NID) details, SMS content, Taxpayer Identification Number (TIN) certificates, passport information, and mobile financial transaction records. These services are advertised and facilitated via platforms like Facebook, Telegram, and WhatsApp.

Prothom Alo first gathered information on this issue in October, collecting several CDRs. Separately, in August, the fact-checking organization Dismisslab published a report identifying 10 active websites and over 600 Facebook posts involved in selling personal data.

Miraj Ahmed Chowdhury, Managing Director of Digitally Right, emphasized that personal communication is highly confidential, and its easy availability infringes upon privacy rights. He warned that criminal groups could exploit CDRs to track individuals' movements and potentially cause harm.

One such website, upon registration, displayed advertisements for services like NID creation, birth registration, biometric orders, location tracking, and call list acquisition. The cost for a three-month CDR was BDT 1,050, while a six-month record cost BDT 1,200.

Post, Telecommunication and Information Technology Minister Fakir Mahbub Anam stated that the government cannot allow citizens' personal data to be sold or leaked. He affirmed that the government is actively working with the Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission (BTRC) and law enforcement to identify and prosecute the perpetrators.

BTRC Chairman Major General (Retd.) Emdad Ul Bari echoed these concerns, calling the sale of citizens' personal data a risk to national security. He confirmed that BTRC is collaborating with law enforcement agencies to address this critical issue.

Mobile operators are legally mandated to store customer data, including call logs, SMS exchanges, IMEI numbers, and cell tower locations used during communication. This comprehensive data, known as CDRs, is typically accessible only to law enforcement and intelligence agencies under strict protocols.
